title: AI Doesn’t Have to Go Rogue to Break the World
summary_raw:
This essay is adapted from a keynote speech delivered at the DEF CON 34 conference in Las Vegas on August 7, 2026. The essay originally appeared in CyberScoop.

I want to talk about AI hacking. There are three aspects: people hacking AI systems, people using AI to hack other systems, and AIs hacking systems on their own, not even maliciously. The last two matter more than the first. The third is the weirdest and potentially the most destabilizing.

I started writing about this in 2021 and in my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind. Back then I said it was mostly still science fiction, but not stupid science fiction. We’re seeing it more and more, especially in the past year. The trends I’m describing don’t require a major breakthrough in AI. They’re starting to happen now, and they’ll happen more often as AIs get better at autonomous problem-solving. And it will involve far more than computer code...

title: Another Way Police Are Locating People from Their Smartphones
summary_raw:
Penlink’s Webloc is an application that locates people using information from the weather, gaming, email, and religious apps on their phone. It’s sold to the police.

The tool collects vast quantities of location data from smartphones via commonly used weather, gaming, email and religious apps. It can build a detailed picture of where a smartphone has been over the past 12 months, and update the data hourly, showing the movements of people on a near real-time basis. Law enforcement officers can use Webloc to zero in on a map and look at all phones that were present at a specific place and time, analyzing “billions of location data points,” according to company documents reviewed by Bloomberg...

title: Pinpointing Location of Videos from Background Airplane Sounds
summary_raw:
This is fascinating:

The video describes a technique that can reveal where an otherwise unidentifiable recording was made by analyzing its audio for the faint sounds of passing aircraft. The technique is both fascinating and frightening.

It works by looking at Doppler curves, which plot the way a plane’s sound changes as it passes overhead because of the Doppler effect. This is the same familiar Doppler effect that causes the frequency of a siren to rise as it approaches and then fall as it passes by and moves away. More generally, it’s the phenomenon whereby the frequency of a wave perceived by an observer changes when the observer and the source of the wave are moving in relation to one another...

title: Announcing XRAID: declustered parity RAID for zoned XFS
summary_raw:
Christoph Hellwig has announced the initial public release of XRAID—declustered parity RAID that is integrated into XFS.

The two primary aims of XRAID are to support parity RAID on zoned devices like SMR hard drives, and to provide a fast RAID implementation without inherent data integrity problems. XRAID, just like zoned XFS also works on conventional hard drives and SSDs. Optimizing for SSD performance has not been a focus, but even without that, writes are up to 20 times faster than mdraid. [...]

Work on XRAID has been ongoing for a year and a half, and while we aren't anywhere near ready for an upstream submission, we are interested in feedback and testing from a wider audience now. The current implementation supports zero to 2 parities. We did experiments with the SnapRAID parity library to support 3 and more parities, and while that is not included in the current version, support for more parities is planned and the code is prepared for it.

The xfsprogs branch includes mkfs support and a new "xraid" utility for managing devices and inspecting an XRAID file-systems. We have also extended Zonar (The zoned file-system visualisation tool) to show how each logical zone maps onto physical zones on devices.

Hellwig gave a presentation at FOSSY in August on this topic; video of the talk does not seem to be available yet, but his slides are available.

title: Glasswing overwhelms maintainers with underwhelming findings (VulnCheck)
summary_raw:
Patrick Garrity of VulnCheck has written a blog post that looks at vulnerabilities found by Anthropic's Project Glasswing since it launched on April 7, and finds it wanting:

Of the 37,966 findings Anthropic reports, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public. Just 217 of those have been marked fixed. The more glaring number is that 4.4% (1,654) of the project's findings have already been marked as duplicates, 7.5x more duplicates than fixes. On top of that, 419 findings have been withdrawn. It seems odd that the ledger now claims a 94.2% true positive rate, up from 90.8% at launch, when more findings have been withdrawn or marked as duplicates than fixed, likely a feedback loop missing to the triage rates listed as "True Positives".

[...] AI is a valuable tool for finding vulnerabilities, and I'm not discounting that. But seven months in, the evidence still doesn't match the launch narrative. The CVEs are a sliver of this year's total, almost none are being exploited, fixes have stalled while duplicates and withdrawals pile up, and the triage burden is shifting onto the open source maintainers Glasswing promised to help. The receipts keep coming in. They still don't reconcile.

title: Introducing Polo: a Wayland MATE compositor

Kerem Söke has announced the 1.0 release of Polo, a Wayland compositor for the MATE Desktop Environment:

The idea is to keep MATE behaving as closely as possible to how it does on X11, rather than changing the desktop to fit a different compositor. [...]

Window management, metacity, workspaces, tiling, XWayland, clipboard and clipman support, multiple monitors, display scaling, hotplugging, screenshots, screen sharing, and session management are all working.

I've also added desktop effects: fade, zoom, zap, spin, squeemize, magic lamp, desktop cube, expo, and wobbly windows.

Söke is looking for people to test Polo, particularly on multi-monitor setups, and report back with problems.

title: [$] C++26 contract confusion
summary_raw: The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) has blessed seven C++ language revisions since 1998. The language is mostly developed by ISO's Working Group 21, which considers proposed additions and amendments, integrates them into a document, and then presents that document to the main ISO body to be voted on as a standard. On October 23, for the first time ever, ISO declined to ratify a document presented by Working Group 21, leaving the future of the C++26 standard in doubt. The decision was driven by controversy around a proposed new "contracts" feature that would add pre- and post-conditions to function signatures.

title: Stenberg: 30 years of Internet transfers with curl
summary_raw:
Daniel Stenberg reflects on the 30th anniversary of the curl project.

libcurl runs in an estimated thirty billion installations today. It is a rough estimate since the majority of all libcurl users never tell us they use it, but we need to find it mentioned in their credit screens, open source license windows or their manuals. A super popular app might use libcurl today and not tomorrow, or vice versa, which can make the numbers shift by several billions overnight. In reality of course, once the pulse raise has calmed down and your ego is content, these numbers do not matter. In our corner of the world, things don't change notably when we go from a thousand installs to billions. We still work with similar people, in similar ways, with similar challenges.

title: In Memoriam: Tim Peters 1952–2026
summary_raw:
Guido van Rossum conveys the sad (and somewhat delayed) news of the passing of Tim Peters.

It's hard to overestimate Tim's influence on Python. He's probably best known for writing the Zen of Python (PEP 20), but to me he was a mentor and language co-designer long before that.

Tim found Python not long after its initial release. His first deed was to convince me that Python should support mixed arithmetic between int and float, because most users would expect them to work that way. And he never stopped contributing.

title: [$] Additional hardening for the glibc dynamic linker
summary_raw: The Node.js project recently had a security vulnerability that affected its Brotli decoder. The bug was a buffer overflow, but the particular way that official Node.js binaries are built for Linux meant that one of the main protections against turning a buffer overflow into remote code execution, address space layout randomization (ASLR) could not be turned on. If ASLR had been enabled, the bug would still be exploitable in theory, but much more difficult to exploit in practice. In response, the GNU C Library (glibc) is considering a new set of tunable settings to allow administrators to forbid programs that do not support ASLR. The new settings, while a welcome hardening measure, may not address the root problem.

USN-9090-1: Apache HTTP Server vulnerabilities
summary_raw:
Zhenpeng Lin discovered that Apache HTTP Server's mod_dav module
incorrectly calculated memory sizes when handling WebDAV locks. An attacker
with permission to create WebDAV locks could possibly use this issue to
cause Apache HTTP Server to crash, resulting in a denial of service.
(CVE-2026-42528)

It was discovered that Apache HTTP Server's mod_vhost_alias module
incorrectly handled certain requests, leading to a one-byte stack buffer
overflow. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue to cause Apache
HTTP Server to crash, resulting in a denial of service, or possibly execute
arbitrary code. (CVE-2026-109163)

It was discovered that Apache HTTP Server's mod_md module incorrectly
handled certain conditions, leading to a NULL pointer dereference. An
attacker could possibly use this issue to cause Apache HTTP Server to
crash, resulting in a denial of service. This issue only affected Ubuntu
20.04 LTS, Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, and Ubuntu
26.10. (CVE-2026-106023)

It was discovered that Apache HTTP Server's mod_http2 module incorrectly
handled certain request headers, leading to heap corruption. A remote
attacker could possibly use this issue to cause Apache HTTP Server to
crash, resulting in a denial of service, or possibly execute arbitrary
code. This issue only affected Ubuntu 20.04 LTS, Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, Ubuntu
24.04 LTS, Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, and Ubuntu 26.10. (CVE-2026-119618)

Feliks Penconek, Yang Song, and JiaSheng He discovered that Apache HTTP
Server could treat the target of some internal redirects from CGI programs
as a CGI program. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue to
execute arbitrary code. This issue only affected Ubuntu 26.04 LTS and
Ubuntu 26.10. (CVE-2026-42356)

title: USN-9068-1: Debian-LAN vulnerability
summary_raw:
Wolfgang Schweer discovered that Debian-LAN configured overly permissive
ACLs for the Kerberos admin server. An authenticated user could possibly
use this issue to change the credentials of other users, leading to
privilege escalation.

title: USN-9089-1: x11vnc vulnerability
summary_raw:
It was discovered that x11vnc created shared memory segments with insecure
permissions. A local attacker could possibly use this issue to obtain
sensitive information or modify screen contents.

title: USN-9088-1: TigerVNC vulnerability
summary_raw:
It was discovered that the TigerVNC viewer stored TLS certificate
exceptions as trusted certificate authorities. A remote attacker could
possibly use this issue to impersonate any VNC server after a user had
added a certificate exception for the attacker's server.

title: USN-9087-1: signing-party vulnerability
summary_raw:
It was discovered that the gpg-key2ps tool in signing-party did not
properly sanitize user IDs before passing them to a shell. If a user were
tricked into processing a specially crafted OpenPGP key, an attacker could
possibly use this issue to execute arbitrary commands.

title: USN-9086-1: SA-Exim vulnerability
summary_raw:
It was discovered that SA-Exim unsafely evaluated the parameters of its
greylisting SpamAssassin rule. An attacker able to write SpamAssassin
configuration files or rules could possibly use this issue to execute
arbitrary code.

title: USN-9085-1: Ruby OpenID vulnerability
summary_raw:
It was discovered that Ruby OpenID sent a request to the claimed identifier
URL before verifying the signature of an OpenID response. A remote attacker
could possibly use this issue to perform server-side request forgery
attacks.

title: USN-9084-1: Radicale vulnerability
summary_raw:
It was discovered that Radicale did not delay failed authentication
attempts when using htpasswd authentication. A remote attacker could
possibly use this issue to obtain user passwords through timing or
brute-force attacks.
